flawed_step: Step 4: inferring that the two componentwise inequalities imply the same inequality between weighted averages despite the averages having different stratum weights.
counterexample: Use 700 equally likely outcomes. Cell counts (successes/total) are: T∩C: 81/87; T∩¬C: 192/263; ¬T∩C: 234/270; ¬T∩¬C: 55/80. Treatment succeeds more often within each stratum, but overall its success rate is 273/350, below the alternative's 289/350.
assessment_summary:
1. [JUSTIFIED] Set a=P(S|T,C), b=P(S|T,¬C), c=P(S|¬T,C), and d=P(S|¬T,¬C); all are defined by the positivity assumptions.
2. [JUSTIFIED] The premises state a>c and b>d.
3. [JUSTIFIED] By conditional total probability, P(S|T)=aP(C|T)+bP(¬C|T) and P(S|¬T)=cP(C|¬T)+dP(¬C|¬T).
4. [NOT JUSTIFIED] One might infer from a>c and b>d that the first weighted average exceeds the second, but their weights P(C|T) and P(C|¬T) need not be equal; componentwise inequalities do not compare averages formed with different weights.
5. [JUSTIFIED] To determine whether this gap merely blocks the attempted proof or makes the statement false, construct a finite space of 700 equally likely outcomes with cell data: T∩C has 81 successes among 87 outcomes; T∩¬C has 192 among 263; ¬T∩C has 234 among 270; and ¬T∩¬C has 55 among 80. These four positive cell sizes total 700 and define valid events.
6. [JUSTIFIED] Within C, P(S|T,C)=81/87=27/29 and P(S|¬T,C)=234/270=13/15, with 27/29>13/15 because 405>377.
7. [JUSTIFIED] Within ¬C, P(S|T,¬C)=192/263 and P(S|¬T,¬C)=55/80=11/16, with 192/263>11/16 because 3072>2893.
8. [JUSTIFIED] Overall, T has 81+192=273 successes among 87+263=350 outcomes, so P(S|T)=273/350.
9. [JUSTIFIED] Overall, ¬T has 234+55=289 successes among 270+80=350 outcomes, so P(S|¬T)=289/350.
10. [JUSTIFIED] Since 273/350<289/350, the claimed overall inequality fails even though both stipulated within-stratum inequalities hold; therefore the statement is false.
